details.benefits: Offers rich, flexible creation options using standard quotes or char arrays.
details.keywords: string literal, char array, initialization

Important Thing Detail.1: Java inherently treats every inline string literal sequence as a fully realized String object instance automatically.

details.concept: A String object is completely immutable; its core content cannot be modified after creation. The JVM references a single internal instance for literals with identical text to save memory space.
details.benefits: Drastically saves memory allocations and ensures absolute string data safety across application paths.
details.syntax:
String s1 = "Welcome";
String s2 = "Welcome"; // Points to same interned string instance
details.keywords: immutable, interned string, string pool, literal optimization

Important Thing Detail.1: Reassigning a String variable (s = 'HTML') does not change the original object data; it simply alters the pointer to look at an entirely new string object.
Important Thing Detail.2: String variables pointing to pure matching literals evaluate to true with standard comparison pointers (s1 == s3) because they share the exact same interned object.
Important Thing Detail.3: Strings created with 'new String()' allocate brand new separate objects, evaluating to false under direct pointer checks (s1 == s2).

details.concept: Because strings are immutable, methods designed to swap characters or break sequences apart always generate a fresh string result, leaving the original copy untouched.
details.benefits: Enables safe, non-destructive parsing and structural edits of text content.
details.syntax:
String clean = "Welcome".replace('e', 'A');
String[] tokens = "Java#HTML".split("#");
details.keywords: replace, replaceFirst, split, delimiter

Important Thing Detail.1: replace: Swaps every single matching character instance or substring inside the targeted string.
Important Thing Detail.2: replaceFirst: Limits the text replacement to only the very first matching sequence it finds.
Important Thing Detail.3: split: Extracts clean text tokens out of a string by carving along specified boundary strings.

topics.title: Matching, Replacing and Splitting by Patterns

details.concept: Utilizing regular expressions (regex) to check input formatting, or perform sweeping edits based on dynamic matching rules.
details.benefits: Provides an expressive syntax to parse and validate complex textual formats.
details.syntax:
boolean valid = "440-02-4534".matches("\\d{3}-\\d{2}-\\d{4}");
String[] tags = "Java,C?C#".split("[.,:;?]");
details.keywords: regex, regular expression, pattern matching, validation

Important Thing Detail.1: The token '\\d' translates into a single digit matcher, while '\\d{3}' looks for exactly three digits in sequence.
Important Thing Detail.2: Brackets like '[+$#]' compile a custom set of options, matching any single character that appears inside those boundaries.

details.concept: Strings are fundamentally distinct from character arrays in Java, but the language provides native utilities to transition back and forth.
details.benefits: Allows fast processing of individual character items before reconstructing a full string value.
details.syntax:
char[] chars = "Java".toCharArray();
String str = String.valueOf(chars);
details.keywords: toCharArray, getChars, valueOf, conversion

Important Thing Detail.1: The 'getChars' method provides a fast way to copy a specific sub-segment of a string directly into an existing target destination array at a designated offset index.

details.concept: The String class offers a collection of static valueOf() methods to transform all forms of primitive numeric fields into readable text instances.
details.benefits: Ensures clean type transformation whenever numeric outputs must be printed or combined with text elements.
details.syntax:
String dStr = String.valueOf(10.2);
String bStr = String.valueOf(true);
details.keywords: valueOf, numeric conversion, string representation

Important Thing Detail.1: The static valueOf method is fully overloaded to accept double, float, int, long, char, and boolean types.

details.concept: Highly flexible alternatives to the rigid String class that allow creators to continuously expand, alter, or insert characters inside a single mutable buffer.
details.benefits: Drastically reduces memory overhead by modifying internal data directly without constantly instantiating new intermediate objects.
details.syntax: StringBuilder builder = new StringBuilder("Welcome");
details.keywords: StringBuilder, StringBuffer, mutable, synchronized

Important Thing Detail.1: StringBuffer uses synchronized modifications, making it safe to access across multiple concurrent processing tasks.
Important Thing Detail.2: StringBuilder is non-synchronized, running much faster when your operations are confined to a single processing task.

details.concept: An array of dedicated, in-place edit tools to modify, append, chop out, or flip character sequences within the active builder object.
details.benefits: Provides fluent, high-performance string building tools without generation garbage objects.
details.keywords: append, insert, delete, reverse, replace

Important Thing Detail.1: append: Tacks new characters or primitive entries directly onto the current end of the builder data.
Important Thing Detail.2: insert: Forces new character components into a precise index location within the existing buffer.
Important Thing Detail.3: delete / deleteCharAt: Chops out a range of index positions or a single item instantly.
Important Thing Detail.4: reverse: Flips the character ordering within the builder.

details.concept: A built-in namespace architecture that neatly bundles a massive library of related core classes and interfaces developed by Java.
details.benefits: Organizes framework utilities effectively, making massive code libraries discoverable and preventing naming conflicts.
details.syntax:
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.*;
details.keywords: API, java.lang, java.util, import namespace

Important Thing Detail.1: java.lang: Contains core foundational language classes (String, Math, Object). It is imported into every file automatically.
Important Thing Detail.2: java.util: Stores the entire collection engine framework alongside scanner tools and core utility classes.
Important Thing Detail.3: java.io: Manages data stream transfers, block readers, and system file handling.

details.concept: Custom namespaces set up explicitly by developers to group related project files and interfaces neatly.
details.benefits: Keeps large enterprise systems highly organized, prevents component naming collisions, and enforces cleaner access boundaries.
details.syntax:
package com.myproject.oop;
public class CustomClass { }
details.keywords: user package, custom namespace, project organization

Important Thing Detail.1: Used to efficiently organize sprawling code bases.
Important Thing Detail.2: Helps avoid name collisions, optimizes readability, and provides fine-grained package access security.

details.concept: A unified architecture consisting of interfaces and classes designed to store and efficiently manipulate groups of elements as container objects.
details.benefits: Provides high-performance data structures and algorithms out of the box, reducing custom development effort.
details.syntax: Collection<String> list = new ArrayList<>();
details.keywords: framework, container, java.util, collection, map

Important Thing Detail.1: Collection Category: Dedicated to storing a simple sequential group of individual element pieces.
Important Thing Detail.2: Map Category: Dedicated to tracking key/value associations for rapid lookups.
Important Thing Detail.3: All core interfaces and classes belong directly to the java.util system library package.

details.concept: The basic methods defined by the root Collection interface to handle adding, removing, and examining elements.
details.benefits: Establishes a uniform set of operations across completely different data structures.
details.syntax:
boolean altered = c.add("item");
c.clear();
details.keywords: add, remove, clear, size, contains

Important Thing Detail.1: Modification methods like add() and remove() return a boolean confirming if the structure changed.
Important Thing Detail.2: The framework includes batch actions like addAll(), removeAll(), and retainAll().
Important Thing Detail.3: Query checks include checking element counts with size(), state checks with isEmpty(), and tracking entries with contains().

details.concept: A design pattern that provides a uniform way to walk sequentially through a data structure without exposing its internal layout.
details.benefits: Allows safe, standardized element traversal across arrays, links, or tree structures seamlessly.
details.keywords: Iterator, traversal, uniform access, hasNext, next

Important Thing Detail.1: The standard collection interface explicitly extends the Iterable interface to supply iterators.
Important Thing Detail.2: hasNext() validates if more entries remain; next() steps forward and returns the item.
Important Thing Detail.3: remove() safely extracts the absolute last item delivered by the next() operation.

details.concept: An ordered collection interface that extends Collection, explicitly allowing duplicate entries and maintaining element insertion order.
details.benefits: Provides precise positional control over element placement and indexing.
details.syntax:
List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>();
list.add(0, 99); // Position-oriented insertion
details.keywords: List, index, ordered collection, duplicates

Important Thing Detail.1: Adds position-oriented tracking methods like get(index), set(index, element), and remove(index).
Important Thing Detail.2: Introduces directional tracking via indexOf(element) and lastIndexOf(element).
Important Thing Detail.3: Provides a dedicated listIterator() tool to traverse back and forth through lists bidirectionally.

details.concept: The two primary concrete implementations of the List interface, each backed by entirely different structural memory designs.
details.benefits: Allows developers to select the ideal class implementation based on application performance needs.
details.syntax:
List<String> al = new ArrayList<>();
List<String> ll = new LinkedList<>();
details.keywords: ArrayList, LinkedList, capacity, random access

Important Thing Detail.1: ArrayList stores items in a dynamic array. Exceeding capacity copies elements into a new, larger array.
Important Thing Detail.2: ArrayList is optimal for fast, random index lookups but gets slow when inserting or deleting items at the start.
Important Thing Detail.3: LinkedList stores elements as linked nodes, making insertions and deletions at the front highly efficient.
Important Thing Detail.4: Using the get(i) index lookup method on a LinkedList is highly inefficient; always use an iterator or a foreach loop instead.

details.concept: Legacy sequential containers that inherit from AbstractList, featuring fully synchronized methods for thread safety.
details.benefits: Prevents memory data corruption when multiple execution threads update a single collection concurrently.
details.syntax:
Vector<String> v = new Vector<>();
Stack<String> st = new Stack<>();
details.keywords: Vector, Stack, synchronization, thread-safe, LIFO

Important Thing Detail.1: Vector matches ArrayList behavior but adds synchronized protection overhead, making it slower for single-threaded uses.
Important Thing Detail.2: Stack directly extends Vector to build a Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) element processing system.
Important Thing Detail.3: Stack operations use push() to add items, pop() to remove the top item, and peek() to view the top item without removing it.

details.concept: Containers designed to hold elements prior to processing, adhering to precise ordering rules.
details.benefits: Simplifies staging logic for tasks that must be processed in specific sequence orders.
details.syntax:
Queue<String> q = new LinkedList<>();
PriorityQueue<Integer> pq = new PriorityQueue<>();
details.keywords: Queue, PriorityQueue, FIFO, offer, poll, peek

Important Thing Detail.1: Standard Queues follow First-In, First-Out (FIFO) rules, adding elements at the tail and pulling from the head.
Important Thing Detail.2: PriorityQueues process elements based on their priority values, pulling the element with the highest priority first.
Important Thing Detail.3: The offer() method inserts elements; poll() extracts the head (returning null if empty), while remove() throws an exception if empty.

details.concept: High-performance data structures built to handle specialized item indexing or to enforce absolute element uniqueness.
details.benefits: Optimizes membership verification and enables immediate value lookups using custom key objects.
details.syntax:
Set<String> s = new HashSet<>();
Map<String, Integer> m = new HashMap<>();
details.keywords: Set, Map, unique, dictionary, key-value

Important Thing Detail.1: A Set acts as an efficient structure to hold groups of non-duplicate elements.
Important Thing Detail.2: A Map behaves like a dictionary, mapping a unique search key to a corresponding value entry.

details.concept: A comparison between ordered index tracking and unique element collection engines.
details.benefits: Clarifies choices between retaining insertion order duplicates or keeping clean, unique datasets.
details.syntax:
// List: order + duplicates allowed
// Set: unique elements only
details.keywords: comparison, ordering, uniqueness, duplicate handling

Important Thing Detail.1: Duplicates: Lists explicitly allow duplicate values; Sets strictly reject duplicate entries.
Important Thing Detail.2: Ordering: Lists preserve an ordered sequence; Sets are generally unordered.
Important Thing Detail.3: Implementations: Lists use ArrayList or LinkedList; Sets use HashSet, LinkedHashSet, or TreeSet.

details.concept: A concrete Set implementation that uses an underlying hash table structure to store unique entries.
details.benefits: Provides near-instant performance for inserting, removing, and verifying elements.
details.syntax: Set<String> hs = new HashSet<>(32, 0.75f);
details.keywords: HashSet, initial capacity, load factor, hashing

Important Thing Detail.1: Uses a default initial capacity of 16 and a standard load factor of 0.75.
Important Thing Detail.2: The load factor dictates how full the set can get before its internal capacity automatically doubles.
Important Thing Detail.3: Elements are stored using hashing, meaning a standard HashSet does not preserve any element ordering.

details.concept: An extension of HashSet backed by a linked list to maintain predictable element sequencing.
details.benefits: Combines the duplicate-free rules of a Set with the reliable insertion ordering of a List.
details.syntax: Set<String> lhs = new LinkedHashSet<>();
details.keywords: LinkedHashSet, insertion order, ordered set

Important Thing Detail.1: Unlike a basic HashSet, elements in a LinkedHashSet are retrieved in the exact order they were inserted.

details.concept: A concrete implementation of the SortedSet interface that guarantees elements are always maintained in a sorted order.
details.benefits: Enables automated, continuous data sorting and range extraction queries.
details.syntax: TreeSet<Integer> ts = new TreeSet<>();
details.keywords: TreeSet, SortedSet, NavigableSet, sorting, comparison

Important Thing Detail.1: Elements can be sorted using their natural ordering via Comparable, or by a custom Comparator.
Important Thing Detail.2: Implements NavigableSet to offer searching options like lower(), floor(), ceiling(), and higher().
Important Thing Detail.3: Includes pollFirst() and pollLast() to safely remove and return the minimum and maximum elements.

details.concept: An association container that maps unique search keys to specific data values.
details.benefits: Enables extremely rapid data retrieval, updates, and removals using custom key identifiers.
details.syntax:
Map<String, String> map = new HashMap<>();
map.put("111-34", "John");
details.keywords: Map, key-value, unique key, put, get

Important Thing Detail.1: While List indices must be integers, Map keys can be any object type.
Important Thing Detail.2: A map cannot contain duplicate keys; each unique key can map to exactly one value.
Important Thing Detail.3: Using put() with an existing key replaces the old value and returns that old value.

details.concept: Map.Entry is a public inner interface defined within the main Map interface, tracking a single key-value pair.
details.benefits: Provides a clean, direct iteration mechanism to examine map keys and values together.
details.keywords: Map.Entry, entrySet, keySet, values, inner interface

Important Thing Detail.1: keySet() returns a Set collection containing all the unique keys from the map.
Important Thing Detail.2: values() returns a standard Collection containing all the value elements from the map.
Important Thing Detail.3: entrySet() returns a Set of Map.Entry instances, allowing developers to query pairs via getKey() and getValue().

details.concept: The three standard concrete implementations of the Map interface, each featuring unique ordering behaviors.
details.benefits: Allows developers to balance structural execution speeds against key sorting requirements.
details.syntax: Map<String, Integer> tm = new TreeMap<>();
details.keywords: HashMap, LinkedHashMap, TreeMap, accessOrder, sorting

Important Thing Detail.1: HashMap is highly efficient for lookups and edits, but its entries are completely unordered.
Important Thing Detail.2: LinkedHashMap preserves entry sequencing, supporting either standard insertion order or recent access order.
Important Thing Detail.3: TreeMap automatically sorts its keys, using either natural Comparable ordering or a custom Comparator.
Important Thing Detail.4: TreeMap implements NavigableMap to offer advanced navigation tools like lowerKey(), floorKey(), and pollFirstEntry().

unitTitle: UNIT 5 - PART 1: ABSTRACT CLASSES AND INTERFACES

details.concept: An abstract class is a generalized superclass that cannot be instantiated using the new operator. It defines what an object must do without fully specifying how it does it, acting as a structural blueprint for subclasses.
details.benefits: Provides high-level abstraction, clusters common features, and eliminates code redundancy across related classes.
details.keywords: abstract modifier, blueprint, general superclass, non-instantiable

Important Thing Detail.1: Abstract methods are denoted using the abstract modifier in the method header and are defined completely without any implementation block.
Important Thing Detail.2: Concrete subclasses moving down the inheritance hierarchy become more specific and are required to provide the actual method implementations.

details.diagram:
graph TD
  Super["GeometricObject (Abstract Class)"] --> Sub1["Circle (Concrete Subclass)"]
  Super --> Sub2["Rectangle (Concrete Subclass)"]

details.concept: The operational rules, compiler restrictions, and data field interactions associated with maintaining abstract classes and methods.
details.benefits: Prevents runtime structural failures by ensuring strict compilation checks on class definitions.
details.syntax:
GeometricObject[] objects = new GeometricObject[10];
objects[0] = new Circle();
details.keywords: compilation rules, non-static, protected constructor, instantiation exception

Important Thing Detail.1: An abstract method cannot be contained inside a non-abstract class; if a class holds abstract methods, it must be marked abstract.
Important Thing Detail.2: If a subclass extends an abstract parent and fails to implement all its abstract methods, that subclass must also be declared abstract.
Important Thing Detail.3: Abstract methods are strictly non-static.
Important Thing Detail.4: Constructors in an abstract class are typically defined as protected because they are only intended to be invoked by subclasses through constructor chaining.
Important Thing Detail.5: An abstract class can be explicitly used as a reference data type to build reference arrays, even though it cannot be instantiated with 'new'.

details.concept: An interface is a class-like construct that acts as a strict blueprint containing exclusively static constants and abstract methods. It specifies a common behavior contract for objects of related or completely unrelated classes.
details.benefits: Enforces generic behavior, establishes a solid contract, supports loose coupling, and helps achieve absolute abstraction.
details.keywords: interface, blueprint, static final, loose coupling

Important Thing Detail.1: The Java compiler automatically injects public and abstract modifiers right before all interface method declarations if omitted.
Important Thing Detail.2: The compiler automatically prepends public, static, and final modifiers right before any defined interface data members.
Important Thing Detail.3: Interfaces compile directly into independent bytecode files exactly like a standard standalone class structure.

details.concept: The relationship layout that establishes inheritance and behavioral implementation pathways between classes and interfaces.
details.benefits: Clearly standardizes structural extensions and behavioral mappings across codebase elements.
details.syntax: class StudentRecord extends Person implements CollegeData { }
details.keywords: extends keyword, implements keyword, class relation, interface relation

Important Thing Detail.1: A class can extend another class using the 'extends' keyword.
Important Thing Detail.2: A class can implement an interface using the 'implements' keyword.
Important Thing Detail.3: An interface can extend another interface using the 'extends' keyword.

details.diagram:
graph TD
  ClassA[class] -->|extends| ClassB[class]
  ClassC[class] -.->|implements| InterfaceA[interface]
  InterfaceB[interface] -->|extends| InterfaceC[interface]

details.concept: An explicit mechanism allowing a single class to implement multiple interfaces simultaneously, inheriting behavioral method descriptors from all parent interfaces.
details.benefits: Bypasses class inheritance limitations to securely pull shared actions from multiple disconnected systems.
details.syntax: public class StudentRecord implements CollegeData, HostelData { }
details.keywords: multiple inheritance, implements, interface grouping

Important Thing Detail.1: Java fundamentally bans multiple inheritance with standard classes to prevent ambiguity.
Important Thing Detail.2: Multiple inheritance is cleanly permitted and achieved in Java exclusively through the use of interfaces.

details.diagram:
graph BT
  StudentRecord["StudentRecord (Class)"] -.->|implements| CollegeData["CollegeData (Interface)"]
  StudentRecord -.->|implements| HostelData["HostelData (Interface)"]

details.concept: A design layout where an interim class implements an interface but only overrides a portion of its abstract methods, leaving the rest to be completed by specialized subclasses.
details.benefits: Enables partial class architecture where baseline behaviors are shared early and remaining implementations are deferred.
details.keywords: partial interface, abstract implementation, deferred methods

Important Thing Detail.1: This layout is structurally possible only when the intermediate class implementing the interface is explicitly declared as an abstract class.

details.concept: The architectural distinctions between using an abstract class blueprint and using an interface behavioral specification.
details.benefits: Guides system designers to choose the optimal abstraction tool based on variable, constructor, and inheritance needs.
details.syntax:
interface Run { }
abstract class Walk { }
details.keywords: comparison, structural differences, abstraction choices, single inheritance

Important Thing Detail.1: Variables: Abstract classes have no restriction on variables; Interfaces mandate all fields must be public static final.
Important Thing Detail.2: Constructors: Abstract classes feature constructors invoked via chaining; Interfaces have zero constructors.
Important Thing Detail.3: Methods: Abstract classes have no method type restrictions; Interfaces require all methods to be public abstract instance methods.
Important Thing Detail.4: Inheritance: Java limits a class to single inheritance for class extension, but allows multiple extensions for interfaces.
Important Thing Detail.5: Root Hierarchy: All Java classes trace back to a single common root class (Object), whereas interfaces have no single root hierarchy.

details.concept: An exception is a runtime error object that signals a major processing disruption or condition that blocks normal application execution.
details.benefits: Keeps the application running normally after an error occurs, preventing abnormal application crashes.
details.syntax:
// Standard crash flow vs Exception handled flow
int result = 10 / 0; // Throws Exception
details.keywords: exception object, runtime error, abnormal termination, flow maintenance

Important Thing Detail.1: If a runtime error occurs at statement 5 in an unhandled 10-statement sequence, the remaining statements (6 to 10) are skipped entirely.
Important Thing Detail.2: Performing proper exception handling guarantees that the rest of the program statements execute successfully despite local faults.

details.concept: Java provides five keywords to explicitly track, catch, route, and manage runtime application exceptions.
details.benefits: Supplies a clean, standard language vocabulary to construct resilient fault-tolerant programs.
details.syntax: try { } catch(Exception e) { } finally { }
details.keywords: try, catch, finally, throw, throws

Important Thing Detail.1: try: Encapsulates code blocks that might actively produce a runtime exception; must be followed by catch or finally.
Important Thing Detail.2: catch: Contains explicit block logic designed to handle a targeted exception type; cannot stand alone without try.
Important Thing Detail.3: finally: Executes critical processing statements regardless of whether an exception arises or gets successfully caught.
Important Thing Detail.4: throw: Used to manually create and explicitly throw a specific exception object out of a code block.
Important Thing Detail.5: throws: Used in method headers to declare possible exceptions that might escape, forcing callers to handle them.

details.concept: The functional try-catch pattern used to wrap error-prone statements and route thrown exceptions into appropriate processing handlers.
details.benefits: Separates the process of error detection (in called methods) from error handling (in calling methods).
details.keywords: try block, multiple catch, exception processing

Important Thing Detail.1: Multiple catch blocks are appended below a single try block when that code space can generate completely different exception types.
Important Thing Detail.2: The order of specified exceptions matters; catching a superclass type before a subclass type triggers a compile error.

details.concept: An optional final block appended to a try-catch engine that is guaranteed to run regardless of how the try block executes.
details.benefits: Guarantees resource cleanup, such as closing open database links, freeing IO streams, or closing files.
details.syntax: try { /* ... */ } finally { /* clean up statements */ }
details.keywords: finally block, resource cleanup, execution guarantees, compilation constraints

Important Thing Detail.1: The finally block must appear at the end of the last catch block; putting it before a catch block breaks compilation.
Important Thing Detail.2: Only one finally clause is permitted per try block structure; multiple finally blocks are illegal.
Important Thing Detail.3: The finally block will execute even if a return statement is triggered inside the try or catch blocks beforehand.
Important Thing Detail.4: If an exception arises that is completely uncaught by any local catch blocks, the finally code executes first before passing the exception up to the caller.

details.concept: The structural categorization of error objects within Java, all extending from a single parent root class.
details.benefits: Allows clean classification of errors to decide whether tracking is enforced at compile time or runtime.
details.syntax: throw new IOException(); // Checked exception
details.keywords: Throwable, checked exception, unchecked exception, system errors

Important Thing Detail.1: Throwable: The absolute root class of the entire Java Exception hierarchy.
Important Thing Detail.2: Checked Exceptions: Inspected by the compiler at compile time; the programmer must handle or declare them, or compilation fails.
Important Thing Detail.3: Unchecked Exceptions (Runtime): Bypassed by compiler checks; occur purely during execution. Handling them is optional but recommended.
Important Thing Detail.4: System Errors: Represented by the Error class; denote severe internal JVM problems (like OutOfMemoryError) beyond user control.

details.concept: The throw keyword is used to manually instantiate and explicitly throw an individual exception instance out of a code section.
details.benefits: Allows programmers to intentionally trip an error response when custom business parameters are violated.
details.keywords: throw keyword, manual throwing, instance generation

Important Thing Detail.1: Requires creating a new instance of an appropriate exception type, often passing an explicit error message string into its constructor.

details.concept: The throws keyword is appended to method headers to openly list all potential checked exceptions that the method might throw during execution.
details.benefits: Alerts calling methods to upcoming errors, forcing them to wrap invocations in try-catch blocks or declare the exception themselves.
details.syntax: public void myMethod() throws IOException, SQLException { }
details.keywords: throws declaration, method signature, checked enforcement

Important Thing Detail.1: The throws keyword does not actually throw an exception; it serves solely as a method signature declaration statement.
Important Thing Detail.2: Multiple checked exceptions can be specified in a comma-separated list following the throws keyword.

details.concept: The complete execution lifecycle built upon three fundamental behaviors: declaring, throwing, and catching an exception.
details.benefits: Establishes a predictable, standardized framework to handle and track down faults across deep execution stacks.
details.keywords: call stack, exception propagation, exception handler, stack unwinding

Important Thing Detail.1: When a method triggers an exception, remaining local logic is skipped and Java searches backward through the call stack for an appropriate handler.
Important Thing Detail.2: If the exception type matches a catch parameter block along the path, it is caught and processed by that handler.
Important Thing Detail.3: If an exception unrolls through the entire call stack without matching a catch block, the application aborts and terminates unexpectedly.
Important Thing Detail.4: Java strictly enforces checked exception handling; a method calling a checked-error source must catch it or declare it via throws.

details.concept: A custom exception is a user-defined exception class created by a developer to track domain-specific application errors.
details.benefits: Improves code debugging by introducing distinct, application-specific exception types instead of generic system errors.
details.keywords: user-defined exception, custom error, class extension

Important Thing Detail.1: Custom exception structures are built by creating a standard class that explicitly extends the core Exception class or any of its subclasses.

details.concept: A thread is a lightweight sub-process, representing the absolute smallest unit of code processing within an application. Multithreading enables multiple threads to run simultaneously.
details.benefits: Saves critical system memory by utilizing a shared memory area instead of allocating distinct, separate memory blocks. It minimizes context-switching delays and ensures that an exception inside one independent thread will not break or crash other threads.
details.syntax:
// Threads run independently inside a shared memory workspace
Thread t = Thread.currentThread();
details.keywords: thread, lightweight sub-process, multithreading, shared memory, thread independence

Important Thing Detail.1: Threads save significant memory overhead because they continuously work within a shared memory space without requesting isolated blocks.
Important Thing Detail.2: Threads are fully isolated from a fault perspective; if a critical exception stops one thread, all surrounding threads continue executing unharmed.

details.concept: A thread continuously travels through explicit operational states during its execution life cycle, tracked via java.lang.Thread.State ENUM constants.
details.benefits: Allows the JVM thread scheduler to systematically balance, pause, track, and execute multiple operations without resource starvation.
details.syntax: Thread.State state = Thread.currentThread().getState();
details.keywords: Thread.State, lifecycle, New, Active, Blocked, Waiting, Timed Waiting, Terminated

Important Thing Detail.1: New: The instance is built but start() has not been invoked yet.
Important Thing Detail.2: Active (Runnable/Running): Triggered by start(); Runnable means waiting for the scheduler to select it, while Running means it is actively executing.
Important Thing Detail.3: Blocked or Waiting: Blocked occurs when waiting for a resource lock (like a printer in use); Waiting means it stays inactive while waiting for a notification.
Important Thing Detail.4: Timed Waiting: The thread lies in a waiting state for a specific span of time rather than forever (e.g., calling sleep()), preventing starvation issues.
Important Thing Detail.5: Terminated/Dead: The run() method exits normally after completion, or terminates abnormally via an unhandled fault. A dead thread cannot be respawned.

details.concept: The central java.lang.Thread class extends Object and implements Runnable, delivering constructors and methods to perform core thread actions.
details.benefits: Provides a comprehensive API to directly query, configure, control, and adjust concurrent processing tasks.
details.keywords: Thread class, Thread API, methods, thread control

Important Thing Detail.1: Execution Control: start() initiates execution; run() defines the execution action; sleep(time) pauses it.
Important Thing Detail.2: Information Retrieval: currentThread() references the active thread object; getName() and getId() fetch tracking data.
Important Thing Detail.3: Coordination & Priority: join() blocks until a target thread dies; setPriority() updates priority; yield() temporarily pauses to let others run.
Important Thing Detail.4: Inter-thread Alerts: notify() wakes up a single waiting thread; notifyAll() wakes up all waiting threads associated with an object.

topics.title: Two ways to create a thread

details.concept: Java provides two separate design mechanisms to build and launch custom concurrent processing paths.
details.benefits: Offers implementation flexibility, allowing developers to choose between clean class extensions or keeping inheritance open by implementing interfaces.
details.keywords: Extending Thread, Implementing Runnable, run override, start invocation

Important Thing Detail.1: Extending Thread: Subclass java.lang.Thread, override run(), instantiate your custom subclass, and call start() to initiate execution.
Important Thing Detail.2: Implementing Runnable: Implement java.lang.Runnable, override run(), pass its instance into a new base Thread object, and invoke start() on that Thread object.
Important Thing Detail.3: The start() invocation is what moves a thread to active and internally triggers the target run() logic.

details.concept: Concurrency synchronization controls multi-threaded access to shared resources, ensuring only one thread can manipulate the resource at a time.
details.benefits: Prevents concurrent thread interference and eliminates unexpected data consistency problems when threads target matching variables.
details.keywords: synchronized keyword, lock management, resource sharing, thread interference, data consistency

Important Thing Detail.1: When multiple threads concurrently target an un-synchronized resource, they can produce erroneous, unpredictable, and broken results.
Important Thing Detail.2: Synchronized areas mark code chunks with the synchronized keyword, anchoring execution safety to a specific tracking object.
Important Thing Detail.3: Only one thread can execute inside blocks synchronized on the same object at any given moment; all other threads are blocked until the occupant exits.

details.concept: Declaring an entire method with the synchronized keyword to lock the parent object instance for any shared usage.
details.benefits: Provides an immediate, clean object-level lock covering the entire scope of a method automatically.
details.keywords: synchronized method, object lock, automatic release

Important Thing Detail.1: When a thread invokes a synchronized method, it automatically acquires the implicit lock for that object instance.
Important Thing Detail.2: The acquired lock is released automatically once the thread completes its task or exits the method space.

details.concept: A specialized code block used to apply synchronization specifically to a targeted resource or isolated line range within a method.
details.benefits: Optimizes performance by letting un-synchronized lines run freely, restricting thread waiting exclusively to the critical lines of code.
details.keywords: synchronized block, localized lock, scope optimization, specific resource

Important Thing Detail.1: If a method contains 50 lines of logic but only 5 lines perform critical updates, a synchronized block can encapsulate just those 5 lines.
Important Thing Detail.2: Placing all method content inside a synchronized block yields identical behavior to a standard synchronized method.

details.concept: Class synchronization is achieved using static synchronized methods, anchoring execution locks to the Class object itself instead of a specific instance.
details.benefits: Guarantees data safety across static fields, locking out concurrent threads even if they access the code via entirely different object instances.
details.keywords: static synchronized, class lock, static methods, universal synchronization

Important Thing Detail.1: While standard synchronized methods lock individual instances, static synchronized methods shift locking to provide synchronization on the class level.

details.concept: Java I/O (Input and Output) is used to process inputs and generate outputs, relying on stream operations to keep file handling tasks fast. I/O streams operate continuously to read or store data persistently into files.
details.benefits: Enables robust, fast handling of persistent file operations within any Java application.
details.syntax:
// Input data passes from Source via System.in into Classes
// Output data passes from Classes via System.out into Destination
details.keywords: I/O Stream, persistent operation, file handling, java.io package

Important Thing Detail.1: Keyboard inputs run via System.in to be read by framework classes.
Important Thing Detail.2: Program text results run via System.out to write out data to the console.

details.concept: A stream is an ongoing sequence of byte data flowing from an origin target to a destination target without any index structures.
details.benefits: Provides a uniform data pipeline model to read or write streams of content from files, devices, or networking sockets.
details.syntax:
InputStream is = new FileInputStream("source.dat");
OutputStream os = new FileOutputStream("dest.dat");
details.keywords: stream, sequence of bytes, byte stream, character stream

Important Thing Detail.1: System.out: Standard output stream attached directly to the system console.
Important Thing Detail.2: System.in: Standard input stream attached directly to the keyboard input.
Important Thing Detail.3: System.err: Standard error stream dedicated to displaying system error messages.
Important Thing Detail.4: Byte Streams: Handle inputs and outputs as 8-bit bytes (e.g., FileInputStream and FileOutputStream).
Important Thing Detail.5: Character Streams: Handle inputs and outputs as 16-bit Unicode characters (e.g., FileReader and FileWriter).

details.concept: Text I/O is built directly on top of basic binary I/O pipelines, introducing an abstraction layer that handles character encoding and decoding automatically.
details.benefits: Allows files to be easily viewed, handled, or edited using basic desktop text utility apps like Notepad.
details.syntax:
Scanner input = new Scanner(new File("temp.txt"));
String line = input.nextLine();
details.keywords: text file, character sequence, automatic encoding, Scanner class

Important Thing Detail.1: The JVM converts internal Unicode values to file-specific encodings when saving a character.
Important Thing Detail.2: The JVM converts file-specific encodings back into Unicode values when loading a character.
Important Thing Detail.3: Scanner acts as a standard input class to load character text lines via an input object pipeline.

details.concept: Binary I/O performs raw, direct bit stream copies of memory data into files without executing any encoding conversions.
details.benefits: Much more efficient to process than text I/O because it bypasses overhead from encoding translations.
details.syntax:
DataOutputStream dos = new DataOutputStream(new FileOutputStream("data.dat"));
dos.writeInt(199);
details.keywords: binary file, memory copy, raw bits, process efficiency

Important Thing Detail.1: If you save a numeric value using binary I/O, the exact bit values sitting in system memory are copied into the file.
Important Thing Detail.2: For example, the byte value 199 is kept as 0xC7 inside memory and appears as exactly 0xC7 inside the raw binary file.

details.concept: A direct comparison between raw byte stream mapping and abstracted character line encoding/decoding workflows.
details.benefits: Helps developers choose between readable text editors and high-speed, portable data storage formats.
details.syntax:
// Text I/O program -> Encoding/Decoding -> File storage
// Binary I/O program -> Direct byte write -> File storage
details.keywords: comparison, encoding translation, processing efficiency, portability

Important Thing Detail.1: Conversions: Text I/O requires continuous character translation; Binary I/O requires zero conversions.
Important Thing Detail.2: Efficiency: Binary I/O is much faster because it avoids encoding/decoding overhead.
Important Thing Detail.3: Portability: Binary files are independent of host machine encoding schemes, making them highly portable.
Important Thing Detail.4: Application: Java compiled .class files are binary, allowing them to run on any JVM across different host platforms.

details.concept: The FileInputStream class extends InputStream to provide raw byte-reading features from local physical files.
details.benefits: Provides a direct, low-level streaming channel to extract byte sequences from a file resource.
details.syntax:
FileInputStream input = new FileInputStream("filename.txt");
int value = input.read();
details.keywords: FileInputStream, byte reading, available bytes, close stream

Important Thing Detail.1: available(): Returns the estimated count of bytes that can be safely read from the file stream.
Important Thing Detail.2: read(): Extracts the next individual byte of data from the input file stream.
Important Thing Detail.3: read(byte[] b): Reads up to b.length bytes from the stream into a target byte array block.
Important Thing Detail.4: close(): Closes the stream and frees up associated system resources.

details.concept: The FileOutputStream class extends OutputStream to write raw data bytes to local file targets.
details.benefits: Supports direct byte saving and file appending modes to modify local contents dynamically.
details.syntax:
FileOutputStream output = new FileOutputStream("filename.txt", true);
output.write(65);
details.keywords: FileOutputStream, byte writing, file append, stream close

Important Thing Detail.1: Constructors allow specifying an optional boolean append flag. If set to true, output data is appended to the end of an existing file.
Important Thing Detail.2: write(byte[] ary): Writes the entire contents of a byte array to the target file destination.

details.concept: DataInputStream implements the DataInput interface, enabling applications to parse raw data bytes into primitive values or strings in a machine-independent way.
details.benefits: Allows primitive field attributes to be read cleanly without requiring manual bit-shifting code.
details.syntax:
DataInputStream inst = new DataInputStream(new FileInputStream("test.txt"));
int i = inst.readInt();
details.keywords: DataInputStream, DataInput, primitive reading, readInt, readUTF

Important Thing Detail.1: readInt(): Consumes 4 incoming bytes to construct and return a standard primitive int value.
Important Thing Detail.2: readChar(): Consumes 2 incoming bytes to return a standard primitive char value.
Important Thing Detail.3: readDouble(): Consumes 8 incoming bytes to return a standard primitive double value.
Important Thing Detail.4: readUTF(): Decodes and reads an inline text string formatted using the standard UTF-8 standard.

details.concept: DataOutputStream implements the DataOutput interface, translating primitive values and strings into byte sequences for output streams.
details.benefits: Guarantees portable primitive data storage across diverse external computing systems.
details.keywords: DataOutputStream, DataOutput, primitive writing, writeInt, flush

Important Thing Detail.1: writeInt(int v): Converts a standard int value into a 4-byte sequence on the stream.
Important Thing Detail.2: writeBoolean(boolean v): Writes a boolean out as a single 1-byte value.
Important Thing Detail.3: writeUTF(String str): Writes a text string using portable UTF-8 encoding patterns.
Important Thing Detail.4: flush(): Forces any cached output bytes out of the stream buffer into the underlying storage.

details.concept: BufferedInputStream overlays a memory buffer onto an existing input stream to read data in blocks, reducing disk access requests.
details.benefits: Speeds up application input tasks by delivering items out of memory cache rather than making frequent disk lookups.
details.syntax: BufferedInputStream bis = new BufferedInputStream(new FileInputStream("test.dat"));
details.keywords: BufferedInputStream, memory buffer, reading cache, disk optimization

Important Thing Detail.1: Reads an entire block of data from disk into a memory buffer at once, minimizing disk reads.
Important Thing Detail.2: Individual data requests are then served straight out of the memory buffer to optimize speed.

details.concept: BufferedOutputStream buffers individual write requests in memory before committing them to disk as a single block.
details.benefits: Improves file-saving performance by minimizing frequent disk write operations.
details.keywords: BufferedOutputStream, output buffer, block writing, flush

Important Thing Detail.1: Individual data updates are written directly to the buffer inside memory first.
Important Thing Detail.2: flush() forces the stream to push cached block updates down into the physical disk destination.

details.concept: The RandomAccessFile class implements both DataInput and DataOutput, allowing data to be read or written at any arbitrary position within a file.
details.benefits: Enables non-sequential file edits, letting you jump directly to any byte position instantly.
details.syntax: RandomAccessFile raf = new RandomAccessFile("test.dat", "rw");
details.keywords: RandomAccessFile, file pointer, seek position, mode r, mode rw

Important Thing Detail.1: Modes: Can be opened under read-only 'r' or read-write 'rw' access behaviors[cite: 1, 8].
Important Thing Detail.2: getFilePointer(): Returns the active byte offset from the start of the file where the next operation will occur.
Important Thing Detail.3: seek(long pos): Moves the internal file pointer to a precise target byte position.
Important Thing Detail.4: If you read a 4-byte integer using readInt(), the file pointer automatically advances 4 bytes ahead.

details.concept: Generics enforce type safety by ensuring collections handle a uniform, homogeneous object type, introduced in JDK 5 to catch type mismatches at compile time.
details.benefits: Makes code stable by shifting data type validations from runtime into compile-time checks.
details.syntax:
List<String> list = new ArrayList<String>();
list.add("hello");
details.keywords: Generics, type safety, compile check, homogeneous container

Important Thing Detail.1: Generic type parameters can only accept reference types; primitive types (like int, float, char) are strictly banned.

details.concept: The structural and programmatic benefits gained by applying generic parameter types to classes and methods.
details.benefits: Eliminates ClassCastExceptions at runtime and removes verbose type-casting code.
details.syntax:
// Without Generics: String s = (String) list.get(0);
// With Generics: String s = list.get(0);
details.keywords: Type-safety, type casting, compile-time validation

Important Thing Detail.1: Type-Safety: Container structures are restricted to holding only a single, designated type of object.
Important Thing Detail.2: No Type Casting: Eliminates the need for manual type casting when pulling items out of a collection.
Important Thing Detail.3: Compile-Time Checking: Validates data types during compilation to ensure type mismatches trigger errors early.

details.concept: A class that features a type parameter placeholder, allowing it to adapt safely to various reference types specified during instantiation.
details.benefits: Enables the creation of reusable, type-safe structures that support automatic boxing and unboxing[cite: 7, 8].
details.keywords: generic class, type parameter, reference type, autoboxing

Important Thing Detail.1: To track primitive integers in generic structures, use object wrappers (e.g., ArrayList<Integer>).
Important Thing Detail.2: Autoboxing automatically wraps a primitive value (like 5) into its corresponding wrapper object (new Integer(5)).
Important Thing Detail.3: Autounboxing automatically unwraps wrapper objects back into raw primitive variables during assignment.

details.concept: Generic methods introduce their own independent type parameters, restricting the scope of those type parameters to the method block.
details.benefits: Allows individual methods to operate on a variety of object types independently of the class's generic scope.
details.keywords: generic method, type parameter scope, method parameters

Important Thing Detail.1: Generic type parameters are fully supported across static methods, non-static instance methods, and class constructors.

details.concept: A raw type refers to using a generic class structure without providing a specific type parameter argument.
details.benefits: Maintains backward compatibility, allowing legacy pre-JDK 1.5 code to compile alongside newer versions.
details.syntax:
List rawList = new ArrayList(); // Raw type usage
List<String> typedList = new ArrayList<>(); // Parameterized type
details.keywords: raw type, backward compatibility, type unsafe, manual cast

Important Thing Detail.1: Raw types lack type-safety guarantees, shifting type errors from compile time into runtime ClassCastExceptions.
Important Thing Detail.2: They require manual type casting when retrieving items, making code less expressive and harder to document.

details.concept: The question mark '?' symbol acts as a wildcard parameter in generics to represent an unknown type match.
details.benefits: Increases method flexibility, enabling parameters to accept a range of generic class variants.
details.syntax: void processElements(List<?> elements) { }
details.keywords: wildcard parameter, question mark, type argument restrictions

Important Thing Detail.1: Wildcards are valid when defining method parameters, fields, return types, or local variable declarations.
Important Thing Detail.2: Wildcards are strictly banned when instantiating a generic class instance, invoking a generic method directly, or declaring a supertype.

details.concept: An unbounded wildcard is defined using List<?>, indicating a collection of a completely unknown or unspecified type.
details.benefits: Useful when method logic relies entirely on the base Object class or does not depend on the specific type parameter.
details.keywords: unbounded wildcard, unknown type, object functionality

Important Thing Detail.1: Ideal for methods whose logic is independent of the underlying type parameter.

details.concept: Upper bounded wildcards restrict an unknown type argument to a specific type or any of its sub-types.
details.benefits: Relaxes variable assignments by letting methods accept collections of a class or any of its extended subclasses.
details.syntax:
List<? extends Number> numList;
public static void drawShapes(List<? extends Shape> lists) { }
details.keywords: upper bound, extends keyword, type restriction, subclass matching

Important Thing Detail.1: Declared using the wildcard character '?' followed by the 'extends' (for classes) or 'implements' (for interfaces) keyword, followed by the upper bound type.

details.concept: Lower bounded wildcards restrict an unknown type argument to a specific type or any of its super-types.
details.benefits: Provides less restrictive access than exact type matches, allowing methods to handle a class alongside its parent types.
details.syntax: List<? super Integer> intSuperList;
details.keywords: lower bound, super keyword, superclass matching, type relaxation

Important Thing Detail.1: Declared using the wildcard character '?' followed by the 'super' keyword, followed by the lower bound type.
Important Thing Detail.2: List<? super Integer> can accept collections of type Integer, Number, or Object, making it more flexible than List<Integer>.

details.concept: JavaFX is an open-source, next-generation client application platform designed for developing rich client applications across desktop, mobile, and embedded systems. It functions as a standalone component built on top of the standard JDK.
details.benefits: Provides a modern, efficient, and fully featured toolkit that streamlines the creation of rich client platforms.
details.syntax: public class MyApplication extends javafx.application.Application { }
details.keywords: JavaFX, open source, client platform, desktop, standalone, client application platform

Important Thing Detail.1: Every single JavaFX GUI program must be defined within a custom class that explicitly extends the core javafx.application.Application parent class.

details.concept: The built-in software characteristics, development tools, and APIs that define the JavaFX ecosystem.
details.benefits: Enables creation of highly expressive GUIs while preserving backward compatibility with older Java interface libraries.
details.syntax:
// Swing Interoperability via SwingNode
SwingNode swingNode = new SwingNode();
details.keywords: Java Library, FXML, Scene Builder, UI controls, CSS styling, Swing interoperability, API

Important Thing Detail.1: Java Library: Composed of native classes and interfaces written entirely in Java.
Important Thing Detail.2: FXML & Scene Builder: FXML is an XML-based declarative markup language used to design enhanced GUIs, which can be visually generated using the Scene Builder tool.
Important Thing Detail.3: Built-in Controls & CSS: Packages standard interactive widgets along with support for web-style CSS formatting.
Important Thing Detail.4: Swing Interoperability: JavaFX applications can embed legacy Swing code using the SwingNode class, easing migration paths.

details.concept: The internal layered architecture of components that coordinate to compile, execute, and render a graphics application.
details.benefits: Separates low-level graphics processing hardware pipelines from the high-level code interfaces handled by application developers.
details.syntax: // Architecture coordinates low level engines silently underneath JavaFX APIs
details.keywords: Architecture, Prism, Glass, Quantum Toolkit, WebView, Media Engine, Scene Graph

Important Thing Detail.1: Scene Graph: The absolute starting construction point holding graphical application primitives termed as nodes.
Important Thing Detail.2: Prism: A high-performance, hardware-accelerated graphics pipeline capable of rendering both 2D and 3D imagery.
Important Thing Detail.3: Glass Windowing Toolkit (GWT): Connects JavaFX to the native OS, managing windows, timers, surfaces, and events.
Important Thing Detail.4: Quantum Toolkit: An abstraction layer that ties Prism and GWT together, making low-level engines available to the JavaFX API.
Important Thing Detail.5: WebView & Media Engine: WebView uses WebKit to render HTML5/CSS content, while the Media Engine utilizes GStreamer for audio/video playback.

details.concept: The runtime operational lifecycle steps managed sequentially by the JVM whenever a JavaFX application is launched.
details.benefits: Provides predictable hooks to initialize background resources and clean up assets during termination[cite: 6, 9].
details.keywords: lifecycle, launch, init, start, stop, Platform.exit

Important Thing Detail.1: Instance Creation: The runtime engine constructs an instance of the target Application class.
Important Thing Detail.2: init(): Executes an empty initialization hook method. It can be overridden, but constructing Stage or Scene objects here is strictly forbidden.
Important Thing Detail.3: start(): The primary graphical entry point method where all custom UI rendering code must be written.
Important Thing Detail.4: launch(): A static method invoked within the main method to start the application lifecycle.
Important Thing Detail.5: stop(): An empty hook method that can be overridden to house cleanup logic.
Important Thing Detail.6: Explicit Termination: The application can be manually terminated at any point using Platform.exit() or System.exit(status).

details.concept: The primary component containment hierarchy required to structure and display a graphical interface screen.
details.benefits: Enforces a clear, decoupled architecture separating the window container from physical scene contents and individual node elements.
details.syntax:
stage.setScene(scene);
stage.show();
details.keywords: Application Structure, Stage, Scene, Scene Graph, Node, Root, Branch, Leaf

Important Thing Detail.1: Stage: A virtual container representing the outer window frame, automatically created and passed to the start() method. Height and width are configurable parameters.
Important Thing Detail.2: Scene: Represents the physical container content area, added to exactly one stage instance at a time. Dimensions are passed to its constructor alongside the root node.
Important Thing Detail.3: Scene Graph: A hierarchical, tree-like data structure composed of nodes representing the visual components.
Important Thing Detail.4: Root Node: The foundational entry node of the scene graph; passing it to the Scene constructor is mandatory. Can be a Group, Region, or WebView.
Important Thing Detail.5: Branch / Parent Node: Classes inheriting from Parent (like Group or Region layout panes) that house lists of nested child nodes.
Important Thing Detail.6: Leaf Node: Terminal nodes without children, representing raw widgets or shapes (e.g., Rectangle, Button, ImageView).

details.benefits: Provides a standard implementation checklist for starting a GUI application[cite: 6, 9].
details.keywords: build steps, instantiate root, configure scene, show stage

Important Thing Detail.1: Step 1: Build the Scene Graph by initializing a designated base Root Node (such as Group or layout Pane) and appending sub-nodes.
Important Thing Detail.2: Step 2: Construct the physical Scene container with defined pixel dimensions, binding the scene graph root inside its constructor.
Important Thing Detail.3: Step 3: Target the provided Stage container window, call setScene() to link the prepared scene, customize options like setTitle(), and trigger show() to render it.

details.concept: Layout container panes belonging to the javafx.scene.layout package, used to automatically organize child nodes into structured alignments on-screen.
details.benefits: Automates node positioning within containers without requiring manual pixel coordinates.
details.keywords: Layout Panes, HBox, VBox, alignment, spacing, padding, fillHeight

Important Thing Detail.1: HBox Layout: Automatically arranges all nested child nodes in a single horizontal row.
Important Thing Detail.2: VBox Layout: Automatically arranges all nested child nodes in a single vertical column.
Important Thing Detail.3: Alignment: Controls internal positioning (e.g., Pos.TOP_CENTER) using setter methods.
Important Thing Detail.4: Spacing & Padding: Spacing sets numeric gaps between individual child nodes; Padding sets whitespace margins between the container border and the nodes.
Important Thing Detail.5: fillHeight / fillWidth: Boolean attributes that determine whether resizable child elements stretch to fill container dimensions.

details.concept: A layout pane designed to display multiple independent text nodes within a single wrapping flow configuration.
details.benefits: Allows rich, multi-styled paragraphs to wrap naturally based on container boundaries.
details.keywords: TextFlow, lineSpacing, textAlignment, wrapping text

Important Thing Detail.1: lineSpacing: A double type property used to define the vertical spacing between wrapping text blocks.
Important Thing Detail.2: textAlignment: Controls paragraph layout alignment; accepts CENTER, JUSTIFY, LEFT, or RIGHT constants.

details.concept: A layout manager that stacks its child nodes directly on top of one another in a layered sequence.
details.benefits: Ideal for overlaying text onto background shapes or graphics.
details.syntax:
StackPane sp = new StackPane();
sp.getChildren().addAll(new Rectangle(100, 50), new Label("Click"));
details.keywords: StackPane, layered layout, node stacking, overlay alignment

Important Thing Detail.1: The node appended first is placed at the absolute bottom of the layout stack; subsequent nodes are layered directly on top of it.
Important Thing Detail.2: Features a single 'alignment' property to control node layout tracking, alongside the static setMargin() method.

details.concept: A layout manager that arranges child nodes into an indexed grid structure composed of rows and columns.
details.benefits: Perfect for assembling uniform data entry forms with aligned input fields and labels.
details.keywords: GridPane, rows, columns, hgap, vgap, gridLinesVisible

Important Thing Detail.1: hgap & vgap: Double parameters representing horizontal cell spacing between columns and vertical spacing between rows.
Important Thing Detail.2: gridLinesVisible: A boolean flag; when set to true, it renders grid boundary lines visible for layout debugging.
Important Thing Detail.3: alignment: Dictates the layout alignment of the grid container within its allocation space.

details.concept: A layout pane that arranges elements in a continuous flow, wrapping them automatically at its boundaries.
details.benefits: Prevents elements from clipping by wrapping items down to the next row or column dynamically.
details.syntax: FlowPane fp = new FlowPane(Orientation.HORIZONTAL, 5.0, 5.0);
details.keywords: FlowPane, wrapping flow, orientation, hgap, vgap, columnHalignment

Important Thing Detail.1: A horizontal orientation wraps child nodes based on the pane's width; a vertical orientation wraps nodes based on height.
Important Thing Detail.2: Provides horizontal/vertical spacing gaps via hgap/vgap, along with alignment properties like columnHalignment and rowValignment.

details.concept: A layout manager that arranges child nodes within a grid of uniformly sized cell regions called tiles.
details.benefits: Maintains uniform cell sizes regardless of varying individual node dimensions.
details.syntax:
TilePane tp = new TilePane();
tp.setPrefColumns(4);
details.keywords: TilePane, uniform tiles, prefColumns, prefRows, tileHeight, tileWidth

Important Thing Detail.1: Configures cell dimensions via prefTileHeight/prefTileWidth and monitors actual dimensions via tileHeight/tileWidth.
Important Thing Detail.2: Manages grid shape structure using prefColumns (for horizontal layouts) or prefRows (for vertical tile layouts).
Important Thing Detail.3: Features horizontal and vertical cell spacing options via hgap/vgap, along with a tileAlignment property.

details.concept: A layout pane that anchors child nodes at fixed pixel offsets relative to its edges.
details.benefits: Maintains node positioning during container resize operations.
details.syntax:
AnchorPane.setTopAnchor(childNode, 10.0);
AnchorPane.setLeftAnchor(childNode, 15.0);

details.concept: A layout manager that partitions its space into five distinct sub-regions: Top, Bottom, Left, Right, and Center.
details.benefits: Provides an ideal structure for standard application windows (e.g., top menu, bottom status bar, center content)[cite: 2, 9].
details.keywords: BorderPane, layout regions, region positioning, top, center, bottom

Important Thing Detail.1: Top / Bottom: Node slots reserved for top header rows or bottom footer strips.

details.concept: Dedicated style classes used to apply color palettes and typographic styling to UI text, shapes, and backgrounds.

circle.setStroke(Color.DARKSLATEBLUE);

details.concept: An alternative styling fill pattern that maps an external graphic file onto shape geometries as an explicit background texture.
details.benefits: Enables complex graphical custom textures on vector nodes.
details.keywords: ImagePattern, texture fill, vector skinning, graphical background

Important Thing Detail.1: Step 1: Load the target image asset by instantiating a regular Image reference variable pointing to the source file.
Important Thing Detail.2: Step 2: Initialize an ImagePattern instance, passing the loaded image object into its constructor.

details.concept: The styling class used to configure text typography attributes, including type family, size, weights, and postures.

details.concept: An event represents an interaction signal generated whenever a user or the operating system alters UI node states.
details.benefits: Forms the foundation of interactive applications by capturing physical actions and translating them into code routines.
details.syntax: // User clicks button -> Event trips -> Source records location
details.keywords: event generation, event source, foreground events, background events

Important Thing Detail.1: Foreground Events: Require direct end-user interaction (e.g., clicking a button, dragging the mouse, typing a key, selecting an item).
Important Thing Detail.2: Background Events: Do not require user input; generated by system alerts, resource events, hardware changes, or timers.

details.concept: The base javafx.event.Event class underpins an array of specialized event sub-classes tailored to specific user interaction patterns.
details.benefits: Provides specific state properties (like mouse coordinates or key characters) based on the event context.
details.syntax: circle.setOnMouseClicked(e -> { // Handles a MouseEvent });
details.keywords: Event types, MouseEvent, KeyEvent, DragEvent, WindowEvent

Important Thing Detail.1: MouseEvent: Tracks pointer actions over a node; captures clicks, presses, releases, moves, entries, or exits.
Important Thing Detail.2: KeyEvent: Indicates keyboard interactions on an active node; tracks key presses, releases, and text inputs.
Important Thing Detail.3: DragEvent: Triggers during mouse drag operations; tracks items moving over or dropped onto target nodes.
Important Thing Detail.4: WindowEvent: Tracks parent layout visibility events; captures window showing, shown, hiding, and hidden states.

details.concept: The structural system that intercepts generated events to determine how the application responds.
details.benefits: Decouples visual control elements from the logic that runs in response to user actions.
details.syntax: // Play Button click -> Target: Button, Source: Mouse, Type: Click
details.keywords: event handler, event target, event source, event type

Important Thing Detail.1: Target: The specific visual node element (window, scene, or node) where the interaction occurred.
Important Thing Detail.2: Source: The specific device or entity that generated the event (e.g., the mouse pointer).
Important Thing Detail.3: Type: The specific interaction variation (e.g., mouse pressed versus mouse released).

details.concept: The sequential propagation path traveled by an event through the scene graph hierarchy upon generation.
details.benefits: Allows parent layout levels to preview, intercept, or modify interaction events before child nodes receive them.
details.syntax: // Phase 1: Route Built -> Phase 2: Trait Down (Filter) -> Phase 3: Trait Up (Handler)
details.keywords: event phases, route construction, event dispatch chain, capturing phase, bubbling phase

Important Thing Detail.1: Route Construction: Constructs the initial event path (Event Dispatch Chain) starting from the base Stage down to the source target node.
Important Thing Detail.2: Event Capturing Phase: The event travels down the dispatch chain from top to bottom. Any registered Event Filters execute during this downward pass.
Important Thing Detail.3: Event Bubbling Phase: The event reverses direction and travels from the target node back up to the stage root. Registered Event Handlers execute during this upward pass.

details.concept: The software components that implement the javafx.event.EventHandler interface to execute application logic for intercepted events.
details.benefits: Enables fine-grained event management by separating downward capture filters from upward bubbling handlers.
details.syntax:
circle.addEventFilter(MouseEvent.MOUSE_CLICKED, filter);
circle.addEventHandler(MouseEvent.MOUSE_CLICKED, handler);
details.keywords: EventHandler interface, Event Filters, Event Handlers, filter vs handler

Important Thing Detail.1: Event Filters: Execute early during the downward Capturing Phase, allowing parent nodes to intercept events before children access them.
Important Thing Detail.2: Event Handlers: Execute later during the upward Bubbling Phase as events return up the hierarchy.
Important Thing Detail.3: Both processing components implement the same core EventHandler interface and override its handle() method.

details.concept: The three programming patterns used to hook event-handling routines into JavaFX interactive controls.
details.benefits: Provides implementation choices, ranging from concise inline blocks to reusable external classes.
details.keywords: Lambda expressions, Anonymous class, Separate class, event registration

Important Thing Detail.1: Lambda Expressions: The most common approach; delivers highly concise, readable syntax for short, one-off event responses.
Important Thing Detail.2: Anonymous Classes: Uses the standard EventHandler interface explicitly inline; common in legacy code or for complex configurations.
Important Thing Detail.3: Separate Standalone Classes: Implements the EventHandler interface in a distinct class definition; ideal for reusing the same response logic across multiple controls.
